metadata.title: Attendance in early childhood education and care programmes and academic proficiencies at age 15 (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata to relate students’ early childhood education and care (ECEC) attendance to later academic proficiencies at age 15. The abstract does not specify whether OECD/PISA sampling weights and replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., student design weights or BRR/jackknife replicates). Because the paper is an OECD report and the abstract does not describe weighting, analysts should consult the report’s methods section for the exact weight variable(s) and variance estimation approach used in the international database. If weights were not applied, results would be less representative of the target populations and standard errors could be misestimated under PISA’s clustered, stratified sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The abstract reports associations between ECEC attendance and later academic proficiencies, but it does not describe how missing data were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion, multiple imputation) or whether any PV-based achievement scores were used in the analysis. This is a reporting gap at the level of the provided text: without the methods section, the missing-data strategy cannot be verified. Given that PISA typically involves complex missingness patterns and PV-based achievement scaling, the absence of explicit documentation prevents a reliable classification of the missing-data handling approach.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 data across OECD countries as described in the abstract; the provided text does not specify the analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., grade/age eligibility, exclusions, or whether only students with complete ECEC-history and proficiency measures were retained).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PISA 2015 to examine whether students’ attendance in early childhood education and care (ECEC) programmes is associated with academic proficiencies at age 15. The abstract indicates that, on average across OECD countries, students who attended ECEC tend to score higher in later academic proficiencies, but the ECEC–proficiency differences become almost nil once students’ socio-economic status (SES) is considered. The report also finds that entering ECEC earlier than the typical starting time is associated with lower proficiencies at age 15, suggesting that earlier entry is not universally beneficial. Finally, the abstract reports that ECEC programme quality indicators are positively associated with later academic skills, and that these relationships vary considerably across PISA countries, emphasizing the role of country-specific policy context and programme quality rather than attendance alone.
